question: What is the main goal of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT)?

options.A: To calculate the correct medication dosage for the child
options.B: To perform a rapid, hands-off visual evaluation from the doorway
options.C: To measure the exact blood pressure and temperature
options.D: To listen carefully to heart murmurs with a stethoscope

explanation: You don't even need to touch the child right away! The PAT is a quick, visual tool you can use from the doorway to size up how sick a little one is. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: A child comes in with chest retractions, nasal flaring, and breathing very fast. Which part of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle does this show?
explanation: Spotting retractions and nasal flaring tells you right away how hard the child is working to pull air in. That's all about their work of breathing! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is a slow heart rate (bradycardia) in a sick baby or child such a red flag?

options.A: It is a normal response to mild fever
options.B: It means the heart muscle is exceptionally strong
options.C: It proves the child is well-conditioned
options.D: It usually indicates impending cardiac arrest

explanation: Unlike adults who might have a slow heart rate because they are fit athletes, sick kids drop their heart rate when their body is failing and running out of oxygen. It's a serious warning sign! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What makes an infant's upper airway much easier to block compared to an adult's?

options.A: A larger tongue relative to the oral cavity
options.B: A much wider trachea and larynx
options.C: Complete rigidity of the upper airway cartilage
options.D: An absence of mucus glands in the pharynx

explanation: Babies have surprisingly large tongues for their little mouths! If their head isn't positioned quite right, that tongue can easily slide back and block their airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: When two rescuers are doing CPR on a child, what is the compression-to-ventilation ratio?
explanation: When you have two people working together on a pediatric patient, you use a 15:2 ratio to get more rescue breaths into the child. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why is letting the chest spring all the way back up between compressions so important during CPR?

options.A: It gives the rescuer time to rest their arms
options.B: It lowers the child's body temperature
options.C: It prevents the ribs from fracturing
options.D: It allows blood to refill the heart chambers

explanation: Think of the heart like a sponge. When you push down, you squeeze blood out; when you let the chest recoil, it refills with fresh blood for the next push! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is a major danger of giving a child too many breaths during resuscitation?

options.A: Causing immediate permanent brain damage from too much oxygen
options.B: Lowering the child's heart rate into normal ranges
options.C: Preventing the lungs from ever collapsing
options.D: Increasing intrathoracic pressure and reducing blood return to the heart

explanation: If you bag a child too fast or too hard, you trap too much pressure inside their chest. That extra pressure actually blocks blood from flowing back to the heart. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why should you avoid tilting an infant's head too far back when opening their airway?

options.B: It always causes immediate cervical spine fractures
options.C: The flexible trachea can kink and cause an obstruction
options.D: It makes it impossible to check the pulse

explanation: An infant's windpipe is soft and flexible. If you tilt their head back too far (hyperextension), the airway actually kinks shut like a bent garden hose! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which sign tells you that a child's breathing problem is getting worse and turning into respiratory failure?

options.C: Loud, powerful crying and high energy
options.D: Rapid, deep breathing with normal skin color

explanation: At first, a struggling child breathes super fast. But once their muscles get too tired, they slow down, breathe irregularly, and turn blue (cyanosis). That's a true emergency! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: A toddler arrives at the emergency unit suddenly drooling, making high-pitched breathing sounds (stridor), and very restless, but has no cough. What should you do first?

options.A: Keep the child calm and avoid invasive examinations
options.B: Immediately force the child to lie flat for an X-ray
options.C: Attempt to visualize the vocal cords with a tongue depressor
options.D: Administer oral fluids immediately to soothe the throat

explanation: This sounds like epiglottitis! If you upset or cry the child, their swollen airway can snap shut completely. Keep them calm in their mother's arms and don't force anything into their mouth. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: If a seriously ill child has a completely normal blood pressure reading, does that mean they are out of danger?

options.A: Fluid resuscitation is definitely not needed
options.B: The child is completely free from danger
options.C: Cardiac output is at its absolute maximum
options.D: The child may still be in compensated shock

explanation: Kids are amazing at squeezing their blood vessels tight to keep their blood pressure looking normal, even when they are crashing. A normal BP doesn't mean they aren't in shock! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard type of shock seen in children?
explanation: You'll hear about hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock in pediatrics—'metabolic shock' isn't one of the classic categories. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the most common heart rhythm seen when a child goes into cardiac arrest?
explanation: Unlike adults who often arrest with a shockable rhythm like VF, children usually arrest after a long period of low oxygen, leading straight to asystole or PEA. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: During a pediatric resuscitation, how often should epinephrine be given?
explanation: Epinephrine is a trusty emergency medication given every 3 to 5 minutes during a code to help keep blood flowing to the heart and brain. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is a major focus of care right after a child's heartbeat and breathing return (after ROSC)?

options.A: Discontinuing all cardiac and respiratory monitoring
options.B: Minimizing secondary brain injury and multi-organ damage
options.C: Withholding all fluids to prevent fluid overload
options.D: Allowing the child's body temperature to rise unchecked

explanation: Getting their pulse back is a huge win, but the job isn't done! Now we have to protect their organs—especially the brain—from further stress and damage. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)

question: Why is developing a fever especially dangerous for a child right after they recover from cardiac arrest?

options.A: It stops all medications from working
options.B: It automatically triggers another cardiac arrest
options.C: It increases the metabolic demand of the injured brain
options.D: It proves the resuscitation attempt failed entirely

explanation: When a child's brain is recovering from lack of oxygen, a fever forces it to work much harder and use up oxygen it simply doesn't have to spare. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)
